# Trajectory Learning Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts II through IV built closure around a fixed model, and @sec-vol3-evaluation ended Part IV by measuring the result: which tasks the agent completes, how reliably, and which layer caused each failure. Part V is the first part that changes the model itself, and it moves none of the three H·S·A exposures. A retrained policy runs the same horizon, carries the same state, and holds the same zero ambient authority, so every envelope, log, and gate of Parts II through IV stays in force. What training can change is how often the model's proposals pass those gates. Changing weights is also the last rung of the intervention ladder for a single agent (@sec-vol3-intro-intervention-ladder), slower, costlier, and harder to reverse than any fix to context, tools, or runtime, so it is reached only for failures that the attribution of @sec-vol3-evaluation-postmortems traces to the policy after those fixes were tried. The evaluation machinery that justifies the climb also supplies its signal. Trajectories its verifiers accepted become the training data, and its release gates decide whether a trained model replaces the one in service.

::: {#pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training .callout-principle title="Verified trajectory post-training"}

**Invariant**: Changing model weights is the slowest and least reversible intervention in an agentic system, and it repairs only the failures that remain after missing context, ambiguous tool schemas, and runtime faults are ruled out. For those failures the training signal is a multi-turn trajectory that deterministic checks outside the model have accepted, including trajectories that recover from errors, because a policy that has seen only error-free paths accumulates errors as the horizon grows. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-flywheel-gap and @sec-vol3-flywheel-curation.

**Implication**: A curation pipeline triages each failure before any training run, admits a trajectory only on evidence produced outside the model, and keeps recovery traces in the corpus alongside clean ones.

:::

Once a trajectory is admitted, the loss must be aimed at the tokens the policy will actually write.

::: {#pri-vol3-action-masked-loss .callout-principle title="Observation loss masking"}

**Invariant**: In a serialized trajectory, observation tokens are written by the environment and not by the policy. Training the model to predict them spends capacity on imitating tools and teaches it to write its own observations instead of yielding the turn to the runtime. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-masking.

**Implication**: The training loss covers only tokens the policy will emit when it runs, meaning its actions, the end-of-turn token that returns control to the runtime, and, when the deployment needs it, its reasoning. Prompts and observations stay in context without contributing loss, and a turn cut off before its end-of-turn token is masked or dropped.

:::

Supervised training imitates trajectories that have already passed a check. Reinforcement learning goes further and lets the policy search against the check itself.

::: {#pri-vol3-verifiable-rewards .callout-principle title="Reinforcement learning against isolated verifiers"}

**Invariant**: Reinforcement learning turns the reward check into the objective. The policy learns whatever the check rewards, including any route by which it can reach and change the check, and it learns nothing the check does not test. The gradient also vanishes unless the policy already succeeds on some attempts and fails on others. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-rlvr-need and @sec-vol3-rlvr-sandboxing.

**Implication**: An RL pipeline runs the verifier in an isolated environment that receives only the policy's output artifact, judges the trained policy on held-out tests the reward never saw, and starts from a supervised policy whose pass rate is above zero.

:::

The three chapters form one pipeline, each consuming what the one before it produced. @Sec-vol3-trajectory-curation triages failures, rebuilds their tasks as resettable fixtures, and admits trajectories through a cascade of checks the agent cannot reach, sorting them into a supervised mix of clean and recovery trajectories and a separate pool of hard negatives. @Sec-vol3-fine-tuning trains on the supervised mix by imitation, with the loss aimed at the policy's own tokens. @Sec-vol3-rlvr starts from that fine-tuned policy, whose nonzero pass rate it needs, and optimizes against isolated verifiers where no demonstration reaches. All three depend on the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}), which makes running a stated check on every trajectory affordable and leaves the soundness of that check as the limit on what training can learn. Weights change how likely a proposal is to pass, never the authority to act on it. Part VI takes the resulting agent from one trajectory to many.
